sources_considered.why: Controlled experiments test whether reducing dataset correlations improves generalization, including for stronger pretrained models.
Confirms publication on March 24, 2022 and acceptance to ACL 2022.
A contemporary position paper includes a concrete RoBERTa experiment and explicitly limits what that example establishes.
Confirms the April 27, 2022 publication date and the paper's position-paper character.
Relevant corroboration, but its underlying preprint dates to 2021; it is not needed as decisive evidence for the chosen 2022 period.
Shows that shuffled language models retain word-order information. Relevant to the stronger claim of no linguistic learning, which the contract does not adopt.
The inspected revision postdates the post, and the role of demonstration labels does not directly establish dependence on spurious training correlations.

evidence_items.explanation: Reducing misleading correlations improved independent-test performance for BERT and stronger RoBERTa and ALBERT models, supporting continued susceptibility in 2022. The same experiments found better generalization from larger models and debiasing, which limits any claim that no genuine progress occurred.

evidence_items.explanation: A sentiment-fine-tuned RoBERTa-large model confidently classified an ambiguous sentence as positive; attribution methods highlighted words associated with positive sentiment. This illustrates persistent cue dependence, although the authors explicitly say the example does not establish prevalence.

unresolved_gaps: The selected studies do not comprehensively test every leading model available on September 23, 2022.
They do not directly measure the full breadth of human semantic flexibility or establish a total absence of meaningful learning.
